title: He descended
hook: the creed says he went down to the dead; the Orthodox icon shows him pulling Adam and Eve out

segments.voice: Yesterday, the atonement: ransom, sacrifice, love's example, victory. Your line was love went all the way. Where did you go one step further? Day three hundred three.

Between Good Friday and Easter Sunday there's a day most people skip over. Saturday. The body is in the tomb. The disciples are hiding. Nothing seems to be happening. But the creed slips in a strange line right there, between buried and rose again. In the old prayer book it reads: "He descended into hell." Many people stumble on it. Hell? Now walk into an Orthodox church at Easter and look at the icon on the stand. Christ, in shining white, standing on two broken doors lying crossed beneath his feet. Around him, scattered keys, snapped locks, loose nails. Below, a dark pit. And with each hand he is grabbing someone by the wrist, an old man and an old woman, and hauling them up out of their tombs. Adam and Eve. Today's word is that line in the creed.
screen: `THE SILENT SATURDAY.` → `HE DESCENDED INTO HELL.` → `BROKEN DOORS, AND TWO WRISTS.`

segments.voice: First, the word hell. In the creed it most likely doesn't mean the place of punishment. It translates the Greek Hades, and the Hebrew Sheol: simply the realm of the dead, where everyone who died was thought to go. That's why many modern versions say he descended to the dead. The creed is saying Jesus really died. He went all the way into death, where every human being goes. The Bible hints at more. First Peter says he "went and preached unto the spirits in prison," and a few lines later that the gospel was preached "also to them that are dead." From those verses grew one of the oldest Christian stories: on Holy Saturday, Christ went down to the dead and set free those who had waited for him, from Adam and Eve on. In medieval England they called it the harrowing of hell, the raid on hell. An ancient Holy Saturday sermon, by an unknown writer, imagines Christ finding Adam and taking his hand, saying, more or less: wake up, sleeper, I didn't make you to be held in hell. Christians read the line in different ways. Orthodox and Catholics generally see Christ freeing the righteous dead. Calvin read it as Christ suffering the full weight of separation from God on the cross. Some churches leave the line out, or say it quietly. Across these readings runs one shared hope: there's no place so dark that God won't go there. The psalm says it best: "If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there." Even there.
screen: `HADES: THE REALM OF THE DEAD.` · `HE REALLY DIED.` · `THE HARROWING OF HELL.` · `NO PLACE TOO DARK.` · then, large: `IF I MAKE MY BED IN HELL, BEHOLD, THOU ART THERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember your dead. Settle, and breathe. Let someone you've lost come to mind. A grandparent, a friend, a parent, anyone. See their face. Notice what you miss. If you pray, you can pray for them, as many Christians do, or give thanks to God for them, as many others prefer. You might picture the icon: a hand reaching down, a wrist grasped, someone lifted up. If you don't pray, just hold them in your mind, with love, for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
He descended. The creed's line that Christ went down to the dead, all the way, and, many Christians say, brought them out.
Your line: even there. Today, remember that there's no low place in your life, or anyone's, that is too far down to be reached. Day three hundred three.

howItsDone: Many churches keep Holy Saturday as a quiet day of waiting; Orthodox Christians sing of Christ trampling down death, and the Easter icon, the Anastasis, shows him lifting Adam and Eve from their tombs.

original.note: Greek: Hades, the unseen realm of the dead. The word behind hell in this line of the creed.

trapdoor: what you thought: the creed says Jesus went to hell to be punished.
what it means: he truly died and went to the dead, and, many Christians say, set free those waiting there.
what a scholar hears: Hades and Sheol, 1 Peter 3:19 and 4:6, and a medieval English word, harrowing: a raid.

notes: 'He descended into hell' as in BCP 1662; many modern ecumenical texts (e.g. ELLC) say 'he descended to the dead'.
The icon description (Anastasis) is standard; confirm details (crossed doors, keys, locks, nails).
Ancient Homily on Holy Saturday: paraphrased; author unknown (sometimes attributed to Epiphanius). Confirm paraphrase.
'Some churches leave the line out': e.g. some Methodist usage (Wesley's Sunday Service omitted it). Confirm.
Practice mentions praying for the dead (common in Catholic, Orthodox, some Anglican practice) and giving thanks (preferred by many Protestants), without ranking.

Softened 'All agree on one thing' to 'Across these readings runs one shared hope', and 'doesn't mean' to 'most likely doesn't mean' for the place of punishment, since some readers (e.g. Calvin) tie the line to bearing God's judgment.
